identifying_markers: Distinct spectacle mark on dorsal hood
first_aid: 1. Keep the victim CALM and completely STILL — do not allow walking or running. Panic accelerates venom spread through the lymphatic system.
2. Immediately IMMOBILIZE the bitten limb with a splint or rigid support, keeping it BELOW heart level to slow venom circulation.
3. Apply a PRESSURE-IMMOBILIZATION BANDAGE firmly (not tightly) over the bite area and wrap upward — do NOT occlude arterial blood flow.
4. REMOVE all rings, watches, bracelets, anklets, and tight clothing near the bite site BEFORE swelling begins.
5. Do NOT cut the wound, suck the venom, or apply ice — these actions cause tissue damage and do NOT remove venom.
6. Do NOT apply a tight TOURNIQUET — it traps venom locally and can cause gangrene and limb loss.
7. MARK the edge of swelling with a pen and NOTE the exact time of the bite for medical staff reference.
8. If the victim shows difficulty breathing or swallowing, place them in the RECOVERY POSITION (on their side) to keep the airway clear.
9. TRANSPORT immediately to the nearest hospital with Polyvalent Anti-Venom Serum (AVS) — call emergency ambulance 108.
10. DO NOT give aspirin, alcohol, herbal remedies, or any traditional medicine — only hospital-administered antivenom can neutralize cobra neurotoxin.
notes: Responsible for the largest number of neurotoxic snake envenomations in India. Part of the 'Big Four'.

identifying_markers: Flat triangular head distinct from neck
Deep brown chain-like circular spots in 3 longitudinal rows
symptoms: Severe immediate burning pain & massive localized swelling
Spontaneous systemic bleeding from gums & bite wound
first_aid: 1. Keep the victim absolutely STILL and DO NOT allow any movement — Russell's Viper venom causes severe internal bleeding when the body is active.
2. Immediately SPLINT and IMMOBILIZE the bitten limb in a natural resting position. Do NOT elevate it above heart level.
3. REMOVE all rings, watches, tight jewelry, and constrictive clothing IMMEDIATELY — swelling can be massive and rapid.
4. Do NOT apply an arterial TOURNIQUET — it causes localized tissue necrosis, gangrene, and potential limb loss with hemotoxic venom.
5. Do NOT cut, squeeze, or suck the wound — this worsens hemorrhage and introduces secondary infection risk.
6. MONITOR and record the victim's urine color — dark red or brown urine indicates acute kidney injury requiring urgent dialysis.
7. APPLY a broad pressure-immobilization bandage over the bite but check that a finger can slide underneath — do NOT block arterial pulse.
8. MARK the expanding edge of swelling with a pen and RECORD the bite time — this data is critical for determining antivenom dosage.
9. If victim shows signs of bleeding from gums, nose, or the wound that won't stop, keep them lying flat and ELEVATE LEGS slightly for shock management.

10. RUSH to the nearest emergency trauma hospital with Polyvalent AVS and DIALYSIS capability — call ambulance 108 immediately. Hospital must perform 20-minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20WBCT) on arrival.
notes: Causes profound coagulopathy and acute renal failure. Part of the 'Big Four'.

region: Rural habitations, agricultural fields, floor sleeping mats (nocturnal)
identifying_markers: Glossy steel-black or dark bluish-brown body
Distinct narrow paired white cross-bands along spine
Enlarged hexagonal vertebral scales down middle of back
symptoms: Painless nocturnal bite (often mistaken for insect bite)
first_aid: 1. TREAT EVERY KRAIT BITE AS A CRITICAL EMERGENCY even if the bite appears painless or no puncture marks are visible — Krait venom is 15x more lethal than Cobra venom.
2. Do NOT wait for symptoms to appear — Krait neurotoxin acts slowly but causes IRREVERSIBLE respiratory paralysis if treatment is delayed.
3. Keep the victim completely STILL and LYING DOWN. Do NOT allow them to walk, sit, or move the bitten limb.
4. IMMOBILIZE the bitten limb firmly with a splint and apply a pressure-immobilization bandage over the entire limb.
5. REMOVE rings, watches, and tight clothing from the bitten limb IMMEDIATELY before delayed swelling begins.
6. Do NOT cut the wound, apply suction, or use ice — these methods are ineffective against pre-synaptic neurotoxin.
7. MONITOR breathing closely — if the victim shows difficulty breathing, gasping, or drowsiness, be prepared to provide MOUTH-TO-MOUTH RESCUE BREATHING.
8. Place the victim in the RECOVERY POSITION (on their side) if they become drowsy or unresponsive, to prevent choking.
9. RUSH to the nearest hospital with AVS and VENTILATOR support — call 108 ambulance IMMEDIATELY. Inform hospital that mechanical ventilation may be required.
10. Do NOT give any oral medicines, food, or water — the victim may lose the ability to swallow, risking aspiration pneumonia. Only hospital-administered Polyvalent AVS can reverse envenomation.
notes: 15x more lethal than Cobra venom. Envenomation occurs almost exclusively at night while victims sleep on the floor. Part of the 'Big Four'.

region: Dry semi-arid regions, rocks, red soil, scrub forests
identifying_markers: White cruciform or bird-foot mark on crown of head
Serrated flank scales that produce raspy sawing noise
first_aid: 1. Keep the victim CALM and completely STILL — any movement can accelerate internal bleeding caused by hemotoxic venom.
2. IMMOBILIZE the bitten limb with a broad splint. Keep it at or slightly below heart level.
3. REMOVE all rings, bracelets, and tight clothing near the bite site BEFORE swelling increases.
4. Do NOT cut the wound, suck venom, or apply a tight tourniquet — these worsen hemorrhagic complications.
5. AVOID giving ASPIRIN, IBUPROFEN, or any NSAID painkillers — these drugs drastically worsen systemic hemorrhage with hemotoxic venom.
6. Apply FIRM PRESSURE over the bite with a clean cloth if there is active external bleeding — but do NOT block arterial flow.
7. MONITOR for signs of internal bleeding: blood in urine, bleeding gums, blood in vomit, or large spreading bruises. Report these to medical staff.
8. MARK the edge of swelling and blistering with a pen and NOTE the exact bite time — this is critical for determining antivenom dosage.
9. Keep the victim lying flat. If showing signs of shock (pale, cold, rapid pulse), ELEVATE the legs slightly above heart level.
10. TRANSPORT urgently to the nearest hospital with Polyvalent Anti-Venom Serum (AVS) — call ambulance 108. Hospital must perform the 20WBCT clotting test on arrival.
notes: Smallest of the Big Four venomous snakes, but causes high morbidity in arid zones. Part of the 'Big Four'.

region: Dense forests, Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, Terai regions
identifying_markers: Chevron band pattern on dark olive-brown body
symptoms: Rapid onset flaccid paralysis within 15-30 mins
first_aid: 1. THIS IS A MAXIMUM EMERGENCY — King Cobra injects the largest volume of neurotoxin of any snake. Paralysis can begin within 15 minutes.
2. IMMEDIATELY call emergency ambulance 108 and inform them of a King Cobra bite — high-dose antivenom and a VENTILATOR must be prepared.
3. Keep the victim absolutely STILL, lying down. Do NOT allow any movement — venom spread accelerates dramatically with physical activity.
4. IMMOBILIZE the bitten limb completely with a rigid splint and apply a firm pressure-immobilization bandage from the bite upward.
5. REMOVE all jewelry, watches, and constrictive clothing from the bitten limb IMMEDIATELY.
6. Do NOT cut the wound, suck venom, or apply ice — King Cobra venom volume is too massive for any extraction method to work.
7. MONITOR breathing every 30 seconds — if the victim shows ANY difficulty breathing, drooping eyelids, or difficulty swallowing, begin RESCUE BREATHING immediately.
8. Place the victim in the RECOVERY POSITION if they become drowsy. Be prepared to perform CPR if cardiac arrest occurs.
9. Do NOT give any oral medicines, food, water, or alcohol — swallowing reflex may be lost, causing fatal choking.
10. TRANSPORT with MAXIMUM URGENCY to a hospital with high-dose AVS capability and ICU ventilator support. Every minute of delay increases mortality risk significantly.
notes: World's longest venomous snake. Venom yield can kill an adult Asian elephant within hours.

region: Bamboo groves, coffee/tea plantations, Western Ghats
identifying_markers: Heat-sensing loreal pit between eye and nostril
symptoms: Intense local burning pain and localized edema
Bruising and blistering around bite mark
first_aid: 1. Keep the victim CALM and STILL — avoid panic and unnecessary movement which accelerates venom spread.
2. IMMOBILIZE the bitten limb with a splint and keep it at or below heart level.
3. Gently WASH the bite area with clean water and mild soap — do NOT scrub aggressively.
4. REMOVE rings, bracelets, and tight clothing from the affected limb BEFORE swelling progresses.
5. Do NOT apply ice, heat, or any chemical substances to the bite wound — these increase tissue damage.
6. Do NOT cut or squeeze the bite site — this introduces infection and worsens local tissue destruction.
7. APPLY a clean, dry dressing over the bite wound and secure loosely with a bandage.
8. MONITOR for signs of spreading swelling, blistering, or unusual bleeding — note the time and progression for medical staff.
9. AVOID aspirin, ibuprofen, and NSAIDs — these interfere with blood clotting which is already affected by pit viper venom.
10. TRANSPORT to the nearest hospital for observation and possible antivenom treatment — call ambulance 108. Hospital should monitor for systemic coagulopathy progression over 24 hours.
notes: Arboreal viper responsible for plantation worker envenomations in southern and western India.

region: Agricultural fields, gardens, urban peripheries, godowns
identifying_markers: Large yellowish-brown body with black net-like tail markings
Large round eyes with golden iris
symptoms: NO neurotoxic or hemotoxic systemic symptoms
first_aid: 1. REASSURE the victim — the Indian Rat Snake is completely NON-VENOMOUS and the bite poses no systemic danger.
2. Gently WASH the bite wound thoroughly with clean running water and mild antiseptic soap for at least 5 minutes.
3. APPLY a mild antiseptic solution (povidone-iodine / Betadine) to the wound to prevent bacterial infection.
4. Cover the wound with a CLEAN, STERILE, DRY DRESSING — change the dressing once daily.
5. REMOVE any rings or tight clothing near the bite area as a precaution, even though significant swelling is unlikely.
6. Check TETANUS vaccination status — if the last Tetanus Toxoid (TT) booster was more than 5 years ago, get a booster shot.
7. MONITOR the wound for 48 hours for any signs of secondary bacterial infection: increasing redness, warmth, pus, or fever.
8. If infection signs appear, visit a doctor for ANTIBIOTIC treatment — not antivenom.
9. Do NOT apply turmeric paste, herbal remedies, or traditional medicines to the wound — these can cause infection.
10. NO ANTIVENOM is needed for Rat Snake bites. Avoid unnecessary hospital visits unless wound infection develops.
notes: Frequently mistaken for Spectacled Cobra due to size and speed, but completely harmless and vital agricultural rodent controller.

region: Scrublands, urban hedges, agricultural tree edges
identifying_markers: Chocolate brown body with dark reticulated cross-bands and white speckling
Dual black streaks radiating from eye
first_aid: 1. REASSURE the victim — the Common Trinket Snake is completely NON-VENOMOUS and the bite is harmless.
2. Gently WASH the bite scratches with clean running water and antiseptic soap.
3. APPLY antiseptic solution (povidone-iodine or similar) to the scratch marks to prevent bacterial infection.
4. Cover with a STERILE GAUZE dressing and secure lightly — change dressing daily.
5. REMOVE any tight jewelry or clothing near the bite as a precaution.
6. Check TETANUS vaccination status — administer a TT booster if the last dose was more than 5 years ago.
7. Take an over-the-counter pain reliever (Paracetamol) if there is mild discomfort — avoid aspirin.
8. MONITOR the wound for 24–48 hours for signs of secondary infection: redness, swelling, pus, or fever.
9. If infection develops, consult a physician for appropriate ANTIBIOTIC treatment.
10. NO ANTIVENOM is needed for Trinket Snake bites. This is a harmless non-venomous colubrid species.
notes: Non-venomous colubrid snake often displaying an 'S'-shaped defensive coil.
